newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Duma vote a blow to would-be Russian oil investors.
newsitem.headline: Duma vote a blow to would-be Russian oil investors.

text.p: Western firms looking to invest in Russia's key oil sector were dealt a heavy blow late Friday, when parliamentarians rejected a list of deposits eligible for development under production-sharing agreements, oil executives and analysts said on Monday.

The decision by the State Duma lower house of parliament to turn down a list of seven reserves in its first reading took Western representatives in Moscow by surprise, and threatened to delay further the recovery in the ailing energy sector.
"I was personally very surprised at the decision," said one Western oil firm representative who asked not to be named. "It was not a controversial list in terms of foreign investment."

Of the seven deposits on the list, only two qualified for foreign participation, and only one -- the Prirazlomnoye deposit on the Barents Sea shelf -- was an oil deposit. The other was a group of gold reserves.

The original list drawn up for the Duma's consideration included over 200 deposits. But strong opposition to the agreements, especially among conservatives and nationalists, has seen the list whittled down to 27.

A conciliation commission was set up to try to push through the list of 27 deposits in smaller batches. But even that has failed to win over opponents to the deal, to the obvious disappointment of potential investors.
"The list has fallen at the first fence, and people involved with the agreements must be disappointed," said Martin Cocker, director of Ernst and Young's CIS energy group in Moscow.
Production-sharing agreements allow Western firms to develop oil in risky countries by financing costs and returns by exporting part of their output.
But conservatives in the Duma object to foreign firms' participation in Russia, saying it would deprive domestic producers of the chance of developing prize untapped assets.
Around $60 billion of potential direct investments over the life of the projects are riding on the outcome of the debate.
Some Western oil representatives put a brave face on Friday's decision, saying that the vote may delay, but not prevent, reserves being developed on a production-sharing basis.

They said the second reading on the list was scheduled next month, and that there was a chance it could be passed then. Bills go through to second and third readings even if defeated in the first reading.
"It's still possible if there is the will," said one.
But others questioned the political will to get the long-delayed list and accompanying legislation passed.
"It seems out of step with the way things were going. It seems quite a serious setback to me," an executive said.
Russian and foreign oil industry sources said production- sharing agreements were vital to the long-term success of Russia's oil sector, which has been in steep decline since the late 1980s.

Output last year slipped two percent to 293 million tonnes (5.9 million barrels per day) -- a small drop relative to dizzying declines earlier in the decade -- but still the lowest level for nearly 30 years.
Mature fields dominate output, and major new investments are needed to reverse the stagnation.
"If we don't have the agreements, I think we will have a serious problem with oil production in Russia. There is already evidence of a resumed decline in output," said one analyst.
Russia is the world's third largest oil producer, but used to be its biggest.

Alexei Mikhailov, chairman of the Duma natural resources committee, said on Friday that merely the oil deposits included in the seven, if approved, could boost output by an average of 30 million tonnes a year (600,000 bpd), or 10 percent of output.
